title: —Pulitzer Crash Course: @Joe Weinberg  —Last 10 Winners Ranked: @Joe ...
transcript: The time has come for one of my favourite annual traditions to talk about the one and only Pulitzer Prize for drama, which is being announced on May 5th. I've done a bunch of Pulitzer videos in the past, including a crash course on how it works, as well as a ranking of the last 10 winners, so I'll link both of those in the caption. A reminder, we're looking at plays from the calendar year of 2024, so nothing that premiered this year so far is eligible. First, I have a list of honorable mentions. These are plays that I think could very well be in the mix, but I don't personally have them on my short list. And then here I have a list of plays that could be contenders, but because of previous productions, I'm not sure if they're eligible. It depends on when they chose to submit it, which we just don't know. So without further ado, here are the top seven that I picked in seventh place. I love you so much I could die, an intimate, heartbreaking piece about grief that I know was not everyone's cup of tea, but I still think there's a case for it. It's very innovative and ambitious in its use of form. And there's also a tie into the 20 20 lockdowns, which I think helps it. Sort of in the same vein, I have three houses, another music driven theater piece that looks back on the 2020 lockdown. Period, through the lens of mental illness and the loneliness epidemic. I feel like a lot of people recognize Dave Malloy as a great composer and a great conceiver of shows, which he is, but I also think he's just a great writer all around, and I would argue that The Book of Three Houses is probably the most impressive written text I've ever seen from him. In fifth place, I have the fires, a play that didn't totally work for me, but I think I was in the minority there, and I still had an immense amount of respect for the raw emotional vulnerability of how this play explores both the present struggles and the generational legacy of being a black gay man in America. In fourth place, Bad Kreuel by Dominique Morisseau, who I think is sorely overdue for a Pulitzer. You might say this one won't get picked because it doesn't take place in America, but similar to public obscenities, which was a finalist last year, the American lens of the protagonist is very much the point of the play. In third place, I have Jordans, a wild roller coaster of a play, which I found super entertaining with its ambitious blend of satire and bizarre surrealism, and using that to provide sharp insight into the experience of being a black person in a predominantly white workspace in modern day America. Number two, I have purpose, which is likely to be eligible because it ran at Steppenwolf Last year, and Steppenwolf tends to submit plays even before they go to New York. If you're curious, I recently posted my full thoughts on this one, which I'll link in the caption. But it is absolutely wild to me that Brandon Jacobs Jenkins does not have a Pulitzer yet. I predicted him last year for the comeuppance and I was wrong. Maybe this will be his year. But in first place, the play that strikes me as the most obvious contender for this prize is the ally. It discusses not only Israel and Palestine, but how we in America specifically discuss it and contend with it. I know people criticize this play for being just like one long debate, but I think it rises above that label partly by being just the best application and execution of the debate play format I think I've ever seen. But it's also a play that is itself about debate and how we navigate discourse in modern day America. For my money, it feels like it should be a no brainer. But the Pulitzers are very difficult to predict, so of course I want to hear everyone else's prediction. What did I miss? What am I underestimating or overestimating? I'm so curious. And happy Pulitzer season!
classificationReason: Pulitzer Prize for Drama predictions video covering 7+ contender plays with no single production as the focus.
